answer: Agents can require each identity to lock a scarce token for a fixed period before its votes count, then cap influence per verified stake rather than per account. Splitting one balance across a thousand aliases does not increase its total weight: each alias must tie its claim to the same costly deposit, which remains slashable if it double-votes. A pigment-marked pulse in the public ledger can reveal when deposits are reused, while a cipher hides private details; the attacker pays capital and opportunity cost for every unit of influence.
